items.prose: A tiny model learns from this 15-token text: "the fund bought gold . the bank sold bonds . the fund sold gold ." Its table counts which token follows which.

parts.question: How many times does "fund" come straight after "the"?

feedback.correct: "the fund" appears twice: in the first and third sentences.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each "the" and read the token after it.

byKey.all-the: You counted every "the". One of the three is followed by "bank", not "fund".

explain.text: The three uses of "the" are followed by fund, bank and fund. So "fund" follows "the" 2 times.

parts.question: "the" appears 3 times, each followed by a token. Using the count from part 1, what is the chance "fund" comes after "the"? Give a fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide by the number of times "the" appears.

byKey.whole-text: You divided by all 15 tokens. The chance counts only the places after "the": 3 of them.
byKey.distinct: You gave the 2 different tokens after "the" equal shares. Count every time "the" appears: fund is 2 of the 3.

explain.text: Count over the row for "the": 2 of its 3 next tokens are "fund". So the chance is $\tfrac23$, about 0.6667.

parts.question: The text never says "the bank sold gold ." Given that "bank" follows "the" with chance $\tfrac13$, what is the chance of that sentence after "the"? Give a fraction, or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance of each pair and multiply.

byKey.zero: A chance of 0 needs a pair the text never contains. Here bank then sold, sold then gold, and gold then the full stop all appear in the text.
byKey.missed-half: You left out "gold" after "sold". "sold" is followed by bonds once and gold once, so that chance is $\tfrac12$.

explain.text: "sold" always follows "bank", "gold" follows "sold" 1 time in 2, and "." always follows "gold". So the chance is $\tfrac13 \times 1 \times \tfrac12 \times 1 = \tfrac16$, about 0.1667.

parts.question: In part 3 the table can write "the bank sold gold .", which the text never says. What is this, and why does it matter for a chatbot?

options.text: A hallucination: true pairs join into a claim nothing supports, and it reads as fluently as a true one
A memory: the bank did sell gold, and the table remembered it from somewhere else
options.why: The text says the bank sold bonds. Nothing it saw says the bank sold gold.

options.text: A bug: a correctly built table could never write a sentence that is not in its text
options.why: A correct table joins likely pairs, so it can write sentences its text never says.

options.text: Harmless: a sentence with a chance as small as this is never written in practice
options.why: One run in six is not rare. A chatbot writes a great many sentences, and some of these get through.

feedback.correct: A hallucination. A chatbot does the same at scale, so its fluent claims need checking.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the sentence with what the text says.

explain.text: The table joined three true pairs into a false claim about the bank. A chatbot is a far larger predictor of likely text, so it can do the same, fluently. That is why its specific claims are checked.

items.prose: A start-up makes a tax chatbot from a base model. Its tax advisers write the example chats, and in every reply they cite a rule number. There is no ranking stage.

parts.question: What habit will the new assistant pick up from these chats?

options.text: Citing a rule number in its replies, as the advisers did
Knowing every current tax rule by heart
options.why: A set of chats gives a way of replying. It is not a full, up-to-date copy of the rules.

options.text: Refusing to answer tax questions at all
options.why: Every example reply answers, so answering is what it imitates.

options.text: No habit, because no ranking stage was run
options.why: The habit comes from the example chats. Rankings would only shape it further.

feedback.correct: It imitates the advisers: a rule number in every reply.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what every example reply has in common.

explain.text: The assistant learns to reply the way the example replies were written. Every one cited a rule number, so it will too.

parts.question: A user asks about a rule that changed after the web text was gathered. Given the habit from part 1, what is the danger?

options.text: A rule number that looks right but is out of date or invented
It stays silent, since it has never seen the new rule
options.why: It has learned to answer with a rule number, so silence is the unlikely reply.

options.text: It somehow cites the new rule correctly
options.why: Nothing it learned from contains the new rule.

options.text: It warns that the rule may have changed
options.why: None of the advisers' chats showed that warning, so nothing taught it.

feedback.correct: It answers in its usual way, with a likely-looking rule number that may be old or made up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Combine the habit with what it has never seen.

explain.text: It never read the new rule, yet it has learned to cite a number every time. So it writes a likely-looking number, old or invented, as fluently as a true one.

parts.question: Using parts 1 and 2, put these fixes in the order of the stage each one changes, earliest stage first.

lines.text: Add newer text, including the new rule, before training starts
Add adviser chats that say "check the current rule on the official site"
Run a ranking stage where raters prefer replies that point to the official source

feedback.correct: Pretraining text first, then example chats, then rankings.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each fix to its stage: text, chats or rankings.

byKey.f2: New text changes the base model, the earliest stage. Chats come after it.
byKey.f3: Rankings are the last stage, after the example chats.

explain.text: Newer text belongs to pretraining, the first stage. Chats that point to the official site belong to fine-tuning, and a preference for such replies belongs to the ranking stage, which comes last.

items.prose: A client asks a firm's chatbot about funds. The reply below is an invented example, and every name in it is invented.

lines: You: Which UK fund had the best return last year, and why?
Chatbot: The Harbourline Value Fund returned 31.4% last year, the best of any UK fund.
Chatbot: Its manager, quoted in a 2023 profile, said: "Patience is our only edge."
Chatbot: Funds charge fees, which reduce what investors keep.
Chatbot: I am confident all of this is accurate.
params.title: An invented example

parts.question: Which lines would you have to verify before quoting them to another client? Tap them.

feedback.correct: The 31.4% and the quote are specific claims to check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a specific figure or a quote.

byKey.l4: That fees reduce what investors keep is general and widely known.
byKey.l5: That line claims confidence; it states no fact about funds.

explain.text: A precise return and a quote from a profile are exactly what a model can invent. The fees line is general; line 5 states no fact at all.

parts.question: Line 5 says the chatbot is confident. Using what you tapped in part 1, what does line 5 add to those two claims?

options.text: Nothing: "I am confident" is likely text, not a check
Proof that both claims are right
options.why: It is written the same way as the claims: as likely text.

options.text: Proof for the figure but not the quote
options.why: It checks neither. Both still need a source.

options.text: A sign that both claims are wrong
options.why: Confident answers are often right. It tells you nothing either way.

feedback.correct: Nothing. Both claims still need a source.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how line 5 was written.

explain.text: Line 5 is likely text after a confident answer. It tells you nothing about the 31.4% or the quote, which still need checking.

parts.question: The chatbot named a "best fund" instead of saying it might not know. Which explanation from training fits best?

options.text: It was trained to give helpful-sounding answers, and confident ones were preferred
It searched every UK fund's results and found the best one
options.why: A model on its own searches nothing. It predicted a likely answer.

options.text: It looked the winner up in a list of facts it keeps
options.why: There is no list of facts inside it. It writes likely text.

options.text: Its makers told it which fund was best last year
options.why: Nothing suggests that. Training rewarded answering, which is enough.

feedback.correct: Fine-tuning and feedback rewarded helpful, confident answers over "I do not know".
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what the later stages of training reward.

explain.text: Example chats and raters tend to reward a helpful answer over "I do not know". That holds unless they were built to teach doubt. So the chatbot names a best fund, sure-sounding, whether or not it knows.
